docs.title: I²C API
docs.text:
Python library that provides abstract classes for I2C master devices (normally dongles such as I2CDriver and similar) to communicate with I2C slaves.

I2C is a simple 2-wire (SDA and SCL lines) protocol commonly used to communicate with environmental sensors, motor and pwm controllers and so on. Multiple devices can be connected on the same I2C bus. One of which is a master/controller device and others are slave/client devices. Multiple master devices can also be connected on the same bus but managing that particular use case is outside the scope of this library. Master always is the one who drives the clock line (CLK), while master and a target slave take turns driving the data (SDA) line. Whichever device drives data line for every byte sent recipient device sends ACK or NACK bit at the end of each byte. Each exchange is known as transaction. And each transaction starts with start condition (S in official documentation) and ends with stop condition (P in official documentation) driven by the master. From standpoint of view of the master transaction consist of mixture of one or more of read or write operations (blocks). If a single transaction has more than one block, blocks are separated by the restart condition (Sr in on official documentation). In EBNF notation it can be written like so

S           = start_condition;
Sr          = restart;
P           = stop_condition;
transaction = S block {Sr block} P;

Both read and write ops are initiated by the master. Master writes 7 bits target slave address following by a bit which indicates that this is a read or write operation. If operation is "read", then master stops driving the data line and then the target slave drives data line in response. If master keep driving the clock and does not issue a stop condition slave must keep sending bytes back. If operation is "write", then master continues driving the data line sending as many bytes as necessary. After completing read or write part master can issue the stop condition and thus and transaction, or it could issue restart condition followed by read or write part.

block       = read_block | write_bloc;
read_bit    = 1;
write_bit   = 0;
read_block  = slave_address_7bits read_bit [byte_from_slave];
write_block = slave_address_7bits write_bit {byte_to_slave};

Notice, that nowhere above we talked about reading or writing registers. Common way to define register write is simply to send write($device_address) followed by write bit and then write($register_address) and then by write($register_value). Register read operation consist of "write" part to the device (write($device_address)) followed by write bit, then write($register_addres) and then stop followed by a start condition or just a restart condition, then write($device_address) followed by a read bit, then read bytes from the slave device. If, for example register value is 16 bits, then write first byte and then second byte.

This library provides three forms of communicating to the slave/controller device. Low level, using something called I2C Language, a more traditional methods I2CMaster::read(...) and I2CMaster::write(...) and registers read/write methods. Let's take a look at them in order.

docs.title: I2C Language
docs.text:
This API allows one to construct arbitrary I2C transactions in a very intuitive way. It relies on the Python type system (such as it is) to constrain function calls only to valid set in the valid order. Thus making it impossible to construct an invalid I2C transaction. Each part of the transaction is a function call which can be chained with a next valid function call. For example lets create a transaction object to read from slave device at address 0x42 one byte register with register address 0x7.

from i2c_api import I2CTransactionBuilder

i2c = I2CTransactionBuilder()
read_reg_transaction = i2c.start().address(0x42).write(0x7).restart().address(0x42).read(1).stop()

Returned object read_reg_transaction is an instance of I2CTransaction class. If we print this object it will look like so:

S().Address(0x42).W().Data(0x07).Sr().Address(0x42).Read(1).P()

Where W() is an indication of the write bit and Data(0x07) is one byte to be sent from the master to the slave device at Address(0x42). Call Read(1) means read one byte from the slave. Valid chain of these function calls can be represented like so:

This transaction can be executed in two ways with the help of I2CMaster class.

from i2c_api import I2CMaster, ExecResults

master = I2CMaster()

results: ExecResults = master.exec(read_reg_transaction)
results: ExecResults = read_reg_transaction.exec(master)

Note, that instance of I2CMaster is to be obtained from another library where it is implemented for your specific dongle. For the sake of flow though we simply write above master = I2CMaster() even though that is invalid since I2CMaster is an abstract class.

Variable results is an instance of ExecResults named tuple. Which for the above example you can access like so:

match results:
    case ExecResults(_, True):
        print(f"Success {results.values()[0]}")

    case ExecResults(_, False):
        print("I2C transaction failed")

Calling results.values() returns list of BitArray where each element corresponds to each appearance of read($n_bytes) call. In the above example we have only one read operation, hence if result is successful, then there is just one element in the .values() list.

To write into a register we can construct transaction object like so

from i2c_api import I2CTransactionBuilder

i2c = I2CTransactionBuilder()
write_reg_transaction = i2c.start().address().write([0x7, 0x11]).stop()

If we print above transaction we will see

S().Address(auto).W().Data(0x07).Data(0x11).P()

Notice that we did not pass slave address in the address() function call, hence in string above it says Address(auto). This allows us to assemble transactions without reference to a particular slave device address. This means that this address would have to be supplied when we execute this transaction.

results = write_reg_transaction.exec(master, 0x42)

results = master.exec(write_reg_transaction, 0x42)

Address passed to the exec(...) function will be applied only to the unfilled address() calls.

Write transaction above does not have any read operation, hence we need to check only if it was a successful or not like so

_, is_success = write_reg_transaction.exec(master, 0x42)

_, is_success = master.exec(write_reg_transaction, 0x42)

Transaction object can be serialized to json, saved to some permanent store and then later restored like so:

from i2c_api import I2CTransaction

tr_json_str = I2CTransaction.to_json(write_reg_transaction)
transaction = I2CTransaction.from_json(tr_json_str)

docs.title: Register access
docs.text:
To farther simplify interation with devices that have concepts of registers as described above

i2c_master = I2CMaster()
reg_data: Bits | None = i2c_master.read_register(
    0x42, RegisterAddress(address=0x07, bus_width_in_bytes=1)
)

Above will read one byte from the register whose address is one byte long 0x07 or return None if transaction fails for any reason.

There is a shortcut for the above though. If register address is one byte wide, then you simply pass register address as an int.

i2c_master.read_register(0x42, register=0x07)

This will raise ValueError if register address is outside of range from 0 to 255.

If register holds let say 4 bytes, then you can read it like so

reg_data: Bits | None = i2c_master.read_register(
    0x42, RegisterAddress(address=0x07, bus_width_in_bytes=1), num_bytes=4
)

Writing register has a bit more moving parts. For example write 0x11 into register 0x07 on device at address 0x42

i2c_master = I2CMaster()
data: Bits | None = i2c_master.write_register(0x42, register=0x7, data=0x11)

It returns data that was written into a device (in this case 0x11) or None if transaction failed for any reason. Like with read_register(...) register address can be an int for one byte wide address or an instance of RegisterAddress. Like with write(...) function above, data can be an int for one byte, array of ints one for each byte or a string representing bit array and optional argument num_bytes will pad it the specific number of bytes or if not provided to the nearest number of bytes to fit payload in.

To confirm that data was acutally written you can set read_back=True (default is False).

data = i2c_master.write_register(0x42, register=0x7, data=0x11, read_back=True)

This will write register and will then read it back. Normally these two operations, register write and then read will be in two separate transaction as not every dongle supports restart between write and read op. If you dongle does support it though you can indicate that you want to use restart and do everything that this function does in one single transaction by setting use_restart=True.

docs.title: Read/Write ops
docs.text:
To hide details I2C protocol you can use methods read($device_address, $num_bytes) and write($device_address, $data, ...) present in the I2CMaster class. These methods encapsulate the whole transaction, that is communications starts with start condition and ends with the stop.

from bitstring import Bits

i2c_master = I2CMaster()
data: Bits | None = i2c_master.read(address=0x42, num_bytes=2)
if data is None:
    print("Error")
else:
    print(data)

If transaction fails for any reason it return None. Otherwise, it returns Bits class from the bitstring library.

Method write(...) returns boolean indicating success or failure of the write operation and it accepts data to be sent in several different forms.

i2c_master = I2CMaster()
is_success: bool = i2c_master.write(0x42, data=0x10)

It is an int, then it will send one byte encoded in that int value. If it is an array of integers, that is understood as array of bytes. Naturally each int has to be a range from 0 to 255 or ValueError is raised.

is_success: bool = i2c_master.write(0x42, data=[0x07, 0x10])

If data is a string, then it has to be a string representation of bit or byte array. For example write(0x42, data=0x07) can be written like so

i2c_master.write(0x42, data="0b111")

Note that 0b111 is only 3 bits wide. This payload by default will be padded with zeroes to nearest whole number of bytes. Thus, above will become 0b00000111. If you want to be padded to a greater number of bytes, let say 2 in this example

i2c_master.write(0x42, data="0b111", num_bytes=2)

This will send two bytes to the slave device 0b0000000000000111 (or 0x0007).
